title: Lucy mission to Trojan asteroids: 5 years of discoveries
site_name: EarthSky | Updates on your cosmos and world
excerpt: NASA’s Lucy mission is now less than a year from reaching the Trojan asteroids near Jupiter. And it has already made some exciting discoveries along the way.
content:
• NASA’s Lucy mission is headed to the Trojan asteroids. These asteroids, traveling ahead of and behind Jupiter in its orbit, have never been explored before.
  • Lucy is now less than a year away from the Trojans. But it has already made several exciting discoveries.
  • These include new findings at other asteroids in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

5 years into the Lucy mission

NASA’s Lucy spacecraft is getting ever closer to its destination, the Trojan asteroids. These are two groups of asteroids that travel ahead of and behind Jupiter in its orbit. Lucy is now less than a year away from meeting its first Trojan. Exciting!

Launched on October 16, 2021, Lucy has been traveling for about five years now. But even though it hasn’t reached the asteroids yet, it has already made several remarkable discoveries, researchers from the Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) said on October 19, 2026.

An ambitious mission to unexplored asteroids

Lucy will be the first mission to explore the Trojan asteroids. Hal Levison at SwRI is the principal investigator of the mission. He said:

Lucy is an ambitious NASA mission, with plans to visit 11 asteroids in its 12-year mission to tour the Trojan asteroids that are located in two swarms leading and trailing Jupiter. As we passed through the main asteroid belt, we visited three asteroids, capturing close-up views of those bodies while performing engineering tests of the spacecraft’s innovative navigation system in advance of the main event to study the Trojans. These relics are effectively fossils of the planet formation process, holding vital clues to deciphering the history of our solar system.

Dinkinesh has a moon

Even though Lucy hasn’t reached the Trojans yet, it has already made several discoveries.

The first was at the asteroid Dinkinesh. Back in 2022, the mission team found that Lucy would come close to the asteroid, which was still unnamed at the time. Dinkinesh is in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

The flyby happened in November 2023. The mission team tweaked the spacecraft’s trajectory so it would fly even closer to Dinkinesh. And there was a surprise waiting for them.

The asteroid had a tiny moon! So now, scientists count that as being two asteroids. But there was yet another surprise.

The little moon, now named Selam, was a contact binary. That is, it had two parts that were joined together. So there were three bodies altogether, not just one.

Peanut-shaped Donaldjohanson

Later, in 2025, Lucy flew past another asteroid, Donaldjohanson. And this time, it was the asteroid itself that was a contact binary.

Donaldjohanson is peanut-shaped, with two large lobes joined together by a smooth “neck.” Simone Marchi, deputy principal investigator for Lucy, said:

The Donaldjohanson flyby revealed many surprises about the small asteroid. For instance, the peanut-shaped, two-lobed structure is connected by a remarkably smooth neck. The asteroid also wobbles, rotating end-over-end once every 10.5 Earth days while rolling around its lateral axis once every 26.5 days.

Gravity assists boot Lucy’s speed

During its journey, Lucy looped back and passed by Earth twice. Why? It might sound counterproductive, but the spacecraft uses Earth’s gravity to gain speed and fine-tune its trajectory.

The first gravity assist was in October 2022. Lucy passed only 220 miles (350 km) above the surface of Earth. This propelled Lucy into a two-year solar orbit. Lucy took images of Earth and the moon to calibrate its instruments.

Later, in December 2024, the second flyby increased its speed relative to the sun by over 16,000 mph (25,750 km/h). That put Lucy on a current path to make its first Trojan encounter in August 2027.

Lucy will make yet another Earth flyby in December 2030. It will then reach the second Trojan swarm of asteroids in March 2033.

When problems arise

With any mission, there can be problems that occur, and Lucy was no exception. Soon after launch, one of its two huge solar panels didn’t deploy properly.

However, mission engineers were able to diagnose the problem and get the solar panel to deploy far enough to save the mission.

Other observations

Lucy has been fortunate to witness some other events too during its journey.

In September 2022, NASA DART probe impacted the near-Earth asteroid Didymos (on purpose, to demonstrate planetary defense technology). And Lucy saw it happen.

In September 2025, Lucy observed the now-famous interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS as it passed through our solar system. 

But there is much more to come, as Levison noted:

Despite these eventful five years, most of Lucy’s mission still lies ahead. The main events start in less than a year as Lucy gets a close-up look at four Trojan asteroid systems: Eurybates and its satellite Queta in August 2027, Polymele and its as-yet-unnamed satellite in September 2027, Leucus in April 2028 and Orus in November 2028.

It will be exciting when Lucy finally reaches the Trojans. None of them have been seen up close before, so what will Lucy find?

Bottom line: NASA’s Lucy mission is now less than a year from reaching the Trojan asteroids near Jupiter. And it has already made some exciting discoveries along the way.
